title: Dmytro Dzhulgakov (@dzhulgakov)
summary:
I’m all pro open benchmarks, but comparing **public** LLM endpoints just doesn’t work unless there’s a confirmed huge user base like OpenAI. In fact, performance may be even anti-correlated with popularity😉 Here’s why 🧵
Quoting @anyscalecompute
📈We’re excited to introduce the LLMPerf leaderboard: the first public and open source leaderboard for benchmarking performance of various LLM inference providers in the market.
Our goal with this leaderboard is to equip users and developers with a clear understanding of the capabilities and limitations of LLM inference solutions, featuring key providers such as @replicate, @awscloud, and @togethercompute!
You can find the leaderboard here:
The LLMPerf leaderboard tracks three main metrics: time-to-first-token, inter-token latency, and success rate.
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) measures the time it takes between the query and the first response of the provider. TTFT is especially important for interactive and streaming applications, such as chatbots.
- Inter-token latency measures the average time between consecutive tokens. This is important for applications that require the entirety of the response to be ready, like summarization tasks or agent use cases.

title: Dmytro Dzhulgakov (@dzhulgakov)
summary:
When comparing the speed of LLMs inference, how long should the prompts and completions be?
Current leaderboards from @ArtificialAnlys or @withmartian use 3:1 prompt:completion ratio. But real-world use cases are 10:1 or even 30:1. Speed and cost differences can be dramatic!
I pulled a sample of different use cases served by @FireworksAI_HQ. The most common is 8-10x more tokens in prompts than in completion. Some use cases get into 20-30x territory. Why is it?
The primary source is RAG - i.e. grounding LLMs in external knowledge or context. Extensive RAG can easily have prompts in thousands or tens of thousands of tokens. Other use cases include:
* Lengthy multi-turn chats with long conversation history
* Summarization tasks where input text is naturally long
* Classification or inline code completion where completion is very short.
How do longer prompts affect inference speed? Processing the prompt is 5-50x faster per token than generating completion because it can be done in parallel. Still, with long prompts, this processing stops being negligible. Caching common prompts across requests or allocating dedicated compute to prompt processing greatly helps.
Long prompts make completion slower too. LLMs have 2 major compute blocks: FFN and Attention. FFN cost is the same per token. Attention is ~quadratic in the sequence length and requires linear memory to store the KV cache.
The magnitude of these effects depends significantly on the model architecture and hardware. As we point out in there’s no one size fit all. We’ve seen multiple X speed-ups from tuning dedicated deployments to specific prompt & completion lengths. Consider this example where a special deployment configuration for long prompt leads to 3X higher throughput and lower latencies than the default short-prompt one (all on the same hardware).
At @FireworksAI_HQ we can help you get the best speed and cost for your unique workload. Reach out to us about your LLM needs.
We’re working with the community to ensure the benchmarks capture a realistic picture. Having workloads with very long prompts is one of the critical factors.

title: Dmytro Dzhulgakov (@dzhulgakov)
summary:
Diffusion... for text, wow 🤯. Here's what it means:
1/ Super-speedy generation on GPUs. Groq/Cerebras are at a disadvantage here. Diffusion models (just like LLM training) are all about FLOPs, great for GPUs. Regular LLM inference is more about memory b/w and needs a lot of tricks to run efficiently.
2/ Different strengths and weaknesses compared from other text models. E.g. overall performance is slightly worse than DeepSeek V2 Lite. But it does much better at "fill-in-the-middle" (FIM) compared to other models. FIM is similar to in-painting for images that Diffusion works great for. Maybe it is time for "vibe-based" edits, where the entire text gets morphed at once, conditioned on the prompt.
What does "diffusion" mean? All current LLMs are "autoregressive", i.e. they generate tokens one at a time left to right. Image/video generation models work differently using "diffusion": they start with noise and iteratively replace the entire image. Here they figured out how to make it work for text.
Btw, people often contrast "diffusion" and "transformer". It's really "autoregressive" vs "diffusion" task formulation. Both use "transformer" or could use another architecture.
Funny enough, there's a body of research in the opposite direction: auto-regressive image generation (i.e. in one pass left-to-right, top-to-bottom).
It's very early, but exciting for where this direction may go, and hope @InceptionAILabs open sources or publishes internals!
Quoting @_inception_ai
We are excited to introduce Mercury, the first commercial-grade diffusion large language model (dLLM)! dLLMs push the frontier of intelligence and speed with parallel, coarse-to-fine text generation.

title: Dmytro Dzhulgakov (@dzhulgakov)
summary:
🧐 What’s inside of @OpenAI's new models and other recent open releases from @deepseek_ai , @Alibaba_Qwen , @Kimi_Moonshot and We spent the past few weeks bringing this never-ending stream of goodness to @FireworksAI_HQ. Let’s dive in👇
All models are mixture of experts (MoE) and have a similar architecture at a high level. It’s no surprise as MoEs are highly efficient on GPUs. Superior quality mostly comes from the high-quality data in pre-training and sophisticated post-training (including RL).
But there are key architecture details that matter a lot for efficiency:
🔑 KV cache size defines how many concurrent generations fit in GPU. DeepSeek and Kimi use the creative MLA attention setup to cut it down. Interestingly, OpenAI models are very efficient too without any fancy tricks: fewer layers, smaller heads
🛝 OpenAI additionally uses sliding window in every other layer, so the practical cost is 2x smaller - even less than fancy MLA!
🚦Sparsity of MoE (fraction of experts activated) determines how well GPU scales with load. OpenAI big model shines here: only 5B active parameters out of 120B. Kimi and DeepSeek are very sparse too, but they’re much larger. Lack of shared expert helps too
📏 gpt-oss models are very shallow: only 24/36 layers vs ~60 standard. Perhaps more layers is not all you need!
📜Qwen shines on long context (Qwen3-Coder is even extendable to 1M). I wonder whether context extension can be pushed further for gpt-oss
👥 DeepSeek is the only one using group-based expert selection; others go for simple Top-K. It’s probably a result of them co-designing their big model with a slower network interconnect: grouping helps to minimize communication with expert parallelism
🔢Many models are natively trained in 8-bit. OpenAI models go further here with the official version having just 4-bit weights (while still doing computation in 16 bit). Post-quantizing is tricky; it’s fantastic to see native support. It also makes GPT-OS easily fitable on a single GPU.

title: Dmytro Dzhulgakov (@dzhulgakov)
summary:
Want to turn any LLM into a classifier or reranker? Just look at token probabilities, e.g. p(yes) and p(no).
Sounds hacky? It's actually legit: we prove that with minimal finetuning (<$5), you get calibration too: the LLM's score correctly reflects "confidence" in each option.
Quoting @FireworksAI_HQ
Most people still think of LLMs as free form text generators. In practice, a huge number of real production workloads are actually classification problems. Things like intent detection, routing, moderation, or picking from a small set of labels.
The interesting part is that you don’t need a separate classification head or a custom model to do this. You can turn any generative model into a classifier by mapping each class to a token and letting the model’s next token distribution act as the class probability distribution.
It stays fully compatible with standard fine tuning. It keeps your inference stack simple. And the best part is that you can get well calibrated class probabilities for as little as a couple of dollars in compute. We used Qwen3 4B, trained with LoRA on Fireworks, and the total cost was around 2$.
Our latest blog breaks down the full workflow. How token based classes work. How calibration naturally emerges during training. And how you can serve high quality classifiers without changing model architecture at all.
If your team is building routing systems, moderation pipelines, intent detection, or any production workflow that depends on confidence scores, this is worth a read:

linked_urls.summary: The blog highlights a critical prompt injection vulnerability in LLM serving stacks where user input containing model control tokens can override system prompts. Because standard tokenizers often merge chat templates and user text into a single string, attackers can forge turn boundaries or system instructions, forcing the model to ignore its original directives. To address this, Fireworks AI introduced the safe_tokenization: true API flag, which ensures strings inside user content are encoded purely as subwords rather than structural token IDs. This opt-in defense preserves all user text without silent modification, guaranteeing that a developer's system prompt remains the authoritative instruction for the model.

title: Dmytro Dzhulgakov (@dzhulgakov)
clean_title: Disaggregated RL training with delta weight sync and Hugging Face buckets
summary:
Thanks for the call out and glad to see that our blog inspired the broader community!
We at @FireworksAI_HQ have been using delta updates to scale RL globally for about a year. Including Composer 2 & 2.5 training in 4 datacenters around the world
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJczVmCbQAAac8U.jpg
Quoting @ClementDelangue
The HF science team just made async RL weight sync ~100x cheaper on bandwidth, and you don't need a shared cluster anymore.
The problem: every RL step, the trainer typically has to sync fresh weights to the inference engine. for a 7B in bf16 that's ~14GB. for a frontier 1T fp8 checkpoint, that's ~1TB; in bf16 it would be ~2TB. per sync.
The insight: between two RL steps, ~99% of bf16 weights are bit-identical. at RL learning rates, the optimizer is whispering and bf16 literally cannot hear most of it. the stored bf16 bits don't change.
What they shipped in TRL: only the changed elements get encoded as a sparse safetensors file, dropped into a Hugging Face Bucket, and fetched by vLLM. on Qwen3-0.6B, per-step payload goes from 1.2 GB to 20 to 35 MB. This is exactly what we built Buckets for: S3-like object storage on the Hub, Xet-backed (so even full snapshots only transfer the changed chunks).
The cherry on top: we ran a FULL disaggregated training where:
- the trainer lived on one box
- vLLM ran inside a Hugging Face Space
- the Wordle environment ran in another Space
- weights flowed through one Hub bucket
no shared cluster. no RDMA. no VPN. no NCCL across clouds. just HTTPS and a bucket.
one GPU + a Hugging Face account is now enough to do real disaggregated RL. multi-replica inference fleets across regions become a small devops exercise, not a research project.
Full write-up:
Open source RL keeps eating the moat!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJWvNSjXgAQ0uuo.jpg
clean_summary:
Thanks for the call out and glad to see that our blog inspired the broader community. At @FireworksAI_HQ, we have been using delta updates to scale reinforcement learning globally for about a year, including training Composer 2 and 2.5 across four data centers.

The HF science team recently made asynchronous RL weight synchronization roughly 100 times cheaper in bandwidth by only encoding and transferring the changed weight elements as sparse safetensors files stored in Hugging Face buckets. This approach drastically reduces per-step payloads, from gigabytes to tens of megabytes, enabling full disaggregated RL training without shared clusters, RDMA, VPN, or NCCL across clouds. With just one GPU and a Hugging Face account, multi-region inference fleets become a straightforward devops task, not a research challenge.

The full write-up details how this setup involves a trainer on one machine, vLLM inside a Hugging Face Space, and the environment in another Space, all communicating via a bucket. This method exemplifies how open source RL continues to push the boundaries of democratizing AI.

clean_title: Measuring serverless API endpoint accuracy with the Artificial Analysis Index
summary:
Running fast is not enough, you need fast AND correct
An excellent addition from @ArtificialAnlys to make sure that the flashy speed numbers are backed by 100% matching accuracy
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HO5sEaJaYAAIWbs.jpg
Quoting @ArtificialAnlys
Announcing the Artificial Analysis Endpoint Accuracy Index, measuring how much of an open weights model's accuracy each serverless API endpoint preserves. We are initiating coverage with GLM-5.2, gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek V4 Pro, with Kimi K3 coming soon
Providers trade off accuracy to optimize for speed and cost. They quantize weights, write custom kernels and tune their inference stacks, and sometimes they simply ship bugs. We are bringing the rigor of our Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index to measuring endpoints, so developers can pick providers on accuracy, not just price and speed
We benchmark each serverless endpoint against our own self-hosted reference deployment of the official weights, where 100% represents matching the reference. An endpoint is at reference parity when its result falls within the 95% confidence interval of the reference. Coverage is live for GLM-5.2, gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek V4 Pro, with Kimi K3 accuracy coverage launching soon
Key elements of the Endpoint Accuracy Index:
➤ Three areas, equally weighted: tool calling (BFCL-500, 500 questions, 3 repeats), scientific reasoning (HLE-250, 250 questions, 10 repeats) and long context recall (AA-LCR-25, 25 questions, 10 repeats). Each subset separates endpoints on the serving choices that drive accuracy differences, with repeats sized for tight confidence intervals
➤ Reference deployment: we self-host the official weights at the lab's recommended precision, following the lab's serving recipe, and publish the complete commands for each reference
➤ Inference parameters: we run the model's highest supported reasoning mode and each endpoint's highest supported output length and context window
➤ Confidence intervals: the parity test accounts for uncertainty in both the endpoint's runs and the reference's runs
➤ Rotating coverage: models enter once sufficient number of providers serve them and exit when a newer version in the same family supersedes them. We benchmark new endpoints as providers launch them and refresh all listed endpoints periodically
➤ Point in time: each result carries the date it was measured, with multi-day benchmarks dated to their final day
Key results for GLM-5.2
➤ Output token limits restrict accuracy. Restrictive limits cut responses off before the model finishes reasoning, and the most restrictive endpoints score half the reference or less on HLE-250
Key results for gpt-oss-120b
➤ Tool call handling separates endpoints. Providers parse and format tool calls differently, and some endpoints score 22% on BFCL-500 against 37% for the reference
➤ Serving configuration changes what the model does at the same requested settings. Some endpoints produce far fewer reasoning tokens at the same configured level, and restricted context windows truncate long context tasks
Key results for DeepSeek V4 Pro
➤ DeepSeek V4 Pro endpoints are more in line with the reference. Majority of the endpoints are at reference parity, and DeepSeek's own first-party endpoint scores slightly above the reference
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HO5WeIjbQAAGVg_.jpg
clean_summary:
Running fast is not enough; accuracy matters too. The Artificial Analysis Endpoint Accuracy Index evaluates how well serverless API endpoints preserve a model's original accuracy across different tasks, so developers can choose providers based on correctness, not just speed and cost.

The index benchmarks endpoints against a self-hosted reference deployment, measuring three key areas: tool calling, scientific reasoning, and long context recall. Results show that token limits and configuration choices significantly impact accuracy, with many endpoints falling short of reference parity, especially on reasoning tasks. DeepSeek V4 Pro endpoints tend to perform closer to the reference, with some even exceeding it, demonstrating the importance of rigorous measurement for reliable model deployment.

summary:
Specialized intelligence is hot in case you didn’t notice:
@harvey’s Tenet

GenSpark’s DeepResearch
… the list goes on
Join the movement with @FireworksAI_HQ training platform
Quoting @harvey
Introducing Tenet, our first model post-trained for legal.
Tenet is a Kimi K3 base that we post-trained with @FireworksAI_HQ on a corpus of publicly available legal data, synthetic data, and human expert data simulating long-horizon legal work.
Training increases Tenet's all-pass rate by 82% on LAB and 22% on LAB Contracts relative to the Kimi K3 base model. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on LAB Contracts and places second on LAB.
These gains generalize to other leading agentic benchmarks including @mercor's Apex Agents - Corporate Law, @crosbylegal's Redline Bench, and @scale_AI's Professional Reasoning Bench.
Tenet is also optimized for token efficiency, operating at less than a fourth the cost of leading foundation models.
We additionally post-trained three specialist models for Tenet to use as subagents:
1) M&A Diligence: post-trained with @baseten on our LAB Diligence environment in an RLM harness, this model is optimized for high-scale, long-horizon tasks.
2) Review Tables: trained with @appliedcompute on our Review Table environment, this model is state-of-the-art and cost-effective at high-volume document review and structured data extraction.
3) Firm Knowledge: trained with @EngramLab on our synthetic law firm environment, this model is optimized to learn and search over a firm's knowledge via memory and structured notes.
More details on model training, environment design, benchmarking, results, and more in the article by @gabepereyra below.
What's next for Harvey’s research?
- Scaling LAB to more jurisdictions, practice areas and workflows
- Scaling compute to bring new generalist models and capabilities to Harvey
More to come soon.

summary:
GLM-5.3-Flash is live on Fireworks on day… 2
Why? Because we take quality very seriously. We found a benchmark discrepancy we couldn’t explain, so we delayed the launch to investigate.
Day 0 (Wed): we saw 2x longer thinking on reasoning-heavy benchmarks (AIME & GPQA) for open source engines compared with @Zai_org API. Same scores, worse token efficiency. Agentic benchmarks looked good.
We decided to investigate further, as overthinking might become a quality problem if max_tokens are reached
Day 1 (Thu): as other non-official providers launched, their APIs had thinking in the range of open-source engines: longer than
We launched a private preview endpoint with disclaimers to a few customers and worked with them to assess quality
Day 2 (Fri): the official API updates. We rerun benchmarks: reasoning is now similarly long, consistent with vllm/sglang. Rest of the benchmarks, both public and internal, check out too.
We launched GLM-5.3-Flash publicly:
More details below

clean_summary: GLM-5.3-Flash is now live on Fireworks after a careful delay to investigate a benchmark discrepancy. Initially, reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME and GPQA showed longer thinking times and lower token efficiency compared to open-source engines, raising concerns about overthinking if maximum tokens are reached. After further testing and API updates, benchmarks became consistent with other models, leading to the public launch. The model features architectural improvements such as a hybrid architecture and Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections, reducing long-context serving costs while maintaining accuracy.

clean_title: Cache hit rate and model token efficiency impact cost more than per-token price
clean_summary:
Periodic reminder: cache hit rate and model token efficiency, measured by the number of turns and reasoning tokens, matter more for cost than the per-token sticker price. Efforts are underway to improve cache hit rate on FireworksAI. A video illustrates the concept.

Quoting @ThibaultJaigu, the same model with the same list price can have a 5.7x difference in actual cost depending on cache performance. For glm-5.2 across six hosts, cache hit rates vary from 18% on FireworksAI to 100% on NebiusT, with the price sheet providing little insight without considering cache hit rate. The key to cost efficiency is cache hit rate.
